definition: Tending to talk a great deal, often more than is needed.
example: After two cups of coffee, my usually quiet uncle became loquacious at breakfast.
nuance: Loquacious simply means fond of talking; garrulous adds a sense of rambling on about trivial things.
prompt: A tour guide leads a group of visitors through an old history museum.
options: The loquacious guide kept talking between exhibits, barely pausing for breath.
The loquacious guide led the whole tour in silence, pointing instead of speaking.
The loquacious guide offered only one brief sentence at each display case.
The loquacious gallery had velvet chairs and gold-framed mirrors.
reasons: Constant chatter from one stop to the next shows a strong urge to talk.
Giving a tour without words is the opposite of being talkative.
Short, sparing remarks describe a reserved speaker, not a chatty one.
Velvet and gold suggest luxury; this word describes people who talk a lot, not rooms.

practice.prompt: A new student shares a seat with a classmate on a long bus ride.
options: My loquacious seatmate was too shy to say a word until we arrived.
My loquacious seatmate chatted about her hobbies for the entire trip.
My loquacious seatmate answered each of my questions with a single nod.
The loquacious bus had plenty of room for everyone's backpacks and coats.
reasons: Shy silence for the whole ride is the reverse of chattiness.
Talking freely for hours on end is exactly what a talkative person does.
Replying with nods instead of words shows reluctance to speak.
Having lots of room means spacious; a vehicle cannot be talkative.
